Newton's Laws of Motion:

Newton's laws of motion are three physical laws that, together, laid the foundation for classical mechanics. They describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it and its motion in response to those forces.
Newton's First Law of Motion –
Newton's first law states that every object will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change its state by the action of a net external force.
Inertia is a tendency of matter by which it continues in its existing state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless that state is changed by an external force.

The tendency of an object to resists changes in its state of motion varies with mass. Mass of an object is a measure of its inertia. The more inertia that an object has the more mass that it has. The light object has less inertia.
Newton's Second Law of Motion –
The second law states that the acceleration of an object depends upon two variables: the net force acting upon the object and the mass of the object.

Thus, the acceleration of an object subject to a net external force is directly proportional to the net force, in the same direction as the net force, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object i.e. a = F/m
Where a = acceleration, F = net force & m = mass or F = m × a ⇒ Force (net) = Mass × Acceleration SI unit of force is newton (N).

1 newton is equal to 1 kilogram metre per second square or 1 newton of force is the force required to accelerate an object with a mass of1 kilogram, 1 metre per second, every second. In other words, a force of one newton produces an acceleration of 1 m.s–² on an object of mass 1 kg.
Newton's Third Law of Motion –
For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

The Force imposed by the first object to other object is known as an action while the force imposed by the second object on the first object is known as reaction. Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion:
Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer, propounded three laws about planetary motion around the sun.
These laws are as follows:
First Law –
All planets move around the Sun in an elliptical orbit, having the Sun at one of the two foci.
Second Law –
A radius vector joining any planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in an equal length of time.
The second law clears that for the same planet, it moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther from the Sun.
Third Law –
The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.

Kepler's third law states P² ∝ a³. That means, for bodies orbiting the Sun, knowing the orbital period (P) allows estimation of the semi-major axis (a) of its orbit. Matter around us exists in three different states—(i) solid,
(ii) liquid, and (iii) gas.
The three states of matter show characteristic mechanical properties (many properties overlap across states):
Solids:
show elasticity and plasticity. Solids are not perfectly rigid; a force is required to deform their shape or size.
Fluids (liquids and gases):
liquids and gases can flow and are therefore called fluids; fluids exert pressure (normal force per unit area).
Liquids (specifically):
show surface tension and capillarity because surface tension is concerned with liquids (gases do not have free surfaces).
Buoyancy/floatation (in fluids):
an immersed body experiences upthrust (buoyant force); objects float iftheir density is less than the liquid and sink if greater.
Elasticity:
Generally, the meaning of a rigid substance is a hard solid which has definite shape and size.
But actually these can be stretched, compressed and deformed.
Even though a rigid steel rod can be deformed by applying sufficient external force.
A force is required to deform the shape or size of a body; deformation may be longitudinal, shear, or volumetric.
After removing the force, the body regains original dimensions only if stress is within the elastic limit; otherwise permanent deformation remains.
The property of any substance by which it tries to gain its normal shape after being stretched or compressed is called elasticity.
"Ability of an object or material to resume its normal shape after being stretched or compressed" is elasticity.
On the basis of the property of elasticity, matters are of two types:
Perfectly elastic substance
- Matter which resumes perfectly its normal state after withdrawing the applied force.
Perfectly plastic substance
- Matter which does not resume its normal state after withdrawing the external force, but deformed forever.
Really no matter is perfectly elastic nor perfectly plastic but lies between the limit of these two properties.
Materials may behave approximately elastic (e.g., quartz) or approximately plastic (e.g., wax) within a certain range; putty and mud are close to ideal plastics.
Stress:
During the application of external force on a matter to change its shape or size, an internal reaction force of equal amount is produced in the opposite direction on every section.
This force tries to resume a normal state of matter. Stress is the restoring force per unit area developed in the body.
If force (F) is applied vertically on a transverse section with the area (A) of matter,
then
Stress = F/A
Its SI unit is newton/metre² (Nm–²), i.e., pascal (Pa).
Strain:
When the shape or size of a matter is changed by applying an external force, the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension (e.g. ΔL/L) is known as strain.
Since, it is a ratio, hence it is dimensionless or without any unit.

Surface Tension:
Surface Tension is the elastic tendency of a fluid surface which makes it to acquire the least surface area possible. It is measured in force per unit length.
Its SI unit is newton/metre (Nm–¹).
The value of surface tension of any liquid depends upon its nature, temperature and the medium present on another side of the liquid surface.
Surface tension decreases with rise in temperature.
It becomes zero at the critical temperature.

When gravity/airflow effects are negligible compared with surface tension, drops/bubbles are approximately spherical. Small raindrops are roughly rounded, but larger raindrops flatten/distort as they fall.
Drops occupy the form in which surface (interfacial) energy is minimum (since creating extra surface area requires energy).
If only surface tension acts on a drop (other effects negligible), it minimizes surface area/surface energy and becomes spherical.
Cohesive and Adhesive Force:
According to molecular theory, every matter is made up of small particles, known as atoms; in many substances, atoms combine to form molecules. These particles attract each other.
Cohesive force is the force of attraction between molecules of the same matter.
Adhesive force is the force of attraction between molecules of different matter.

The adhesive force between oil and water is less than the cohesive force of water but higher than cohesive force of oil, so when the water dropped on oil surface, its drops occupy spherical shape by shrinking, while when oil dropped on the water surface, it spreads widely in form of the thin film generally.

Capillarity:
A capillary tube is a narrow tube (commonly glass) of very small internal diameter, open at both ends.
The rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension (with wetting/non-wetting effects) is called capillarity.
Liquids that wet glass (acute contact angle) show capillary rise, while liquids that do not wet glass (e.g., mercury in glass) show capillary depression.
Example: When a capillary tube is kept standing in mercury, the mercury level in the tube is depressed compared with the level of mercury outside.
Examples of capillarity / capillary effects:
In a fountain pen, ink is drawn toward the nib through narrow channels/slits by capillary action.
Fuel/oil rises in candle and lamp wicks by capillary action.
Blotting paper absorbs spilled liquid due to capillary action in its pores.
In plants, water moves upward through xylem mainly due to cohesion–adhesion and transpiration pull; capillarity alone is not sufficient to explain rise to great heights.
Viscosity:

A liquid is flowing over a rigid horizontal surface AB as shown in the figure. The liquid layer which is in contact with the bottom remains at rest/has zero velocity relative to the surface, but the velocity of the upper layers is increasing. The uppermost layer flows with maximum velocity.
In three horizontal layers a, band c, a is with minimum velocity, b has more than a and c is with maximum velocity.
The consecutive layers, from bottom to surface try to reduce the relative velocity between adjacent layers.
An internal force acts between layers, try to slow down the velocity of the layer which is just above it.
An internal force acts on different layers which tries to oppose their relative velocity.
This force is known as the viscous force.
To maintain the flow of liquid, the external force is applied against viscous force.
The property of fluids (liquids and gases), which opposes the relative movement among different layers of fluid, is known as viscosity.
Highly viscous liquids like honey and glycerine have greater resistance to flow, so they flow less readily/slower, than low-viscosity fluids.
With increase in temperature, viscosity of liquids / generally decreases.
The viscosity of gases generally increases with increase in temperature.
Viscosity is primarily a property of fluids; solids generally lack viscosity and mainly resist shear elastically, though some solid materials show viscoelastic/creep behaviour.

It states that the upward (buoyant) force that is exerted on a body immersed in a liquid, whether fully or partially submerged, is equal to the weight of the liquid that the body displaces and it acts in the upward direction at the centre of mass of the displaced liquid.

Visible light is electromagnetic radiation detectable by the human eye. It lies between infrared (longer wavelengths) and ultraviolet (shorter wavelengths).
Wavelength range (approx.): about 380–700 nm (≈ 3.8×10–⁷ – 7.0×10–⁷ m). Some texts extend the upper limit to about 760 nm depending on convention.
Light is perceived only when light from a source/object enters the eyes. Objects are seen because they emit light or reflect/scatter incident light into our eyes.

In a homogeneous medium, under geometrical optics conditions (objects and apertures >> wavelength), light travels approximately in straight lines; light can also diffract (spread/bend) around obstacles and apertures.
Light can travel through a vacuum (sound waves cannot).
Light shows wave–particle duality (wave-like and particle like behaviour).
Thus, light has dual nature:
Particle nature –
behaves in the form of particles.
Wave nature –
behaves in the form of waves.
Speed of light in different media (approx.)
The speed of light depends on the medium and is maximum in vacuum.
Refractive Index:
The refractive index of a medium is equal to the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in that medium.
If the refractive index of a medium is η(m) and the speed of light is v and c in that medium and vacuum respectively, then c

A higher refractive index corresponds to a lower speed of light in that medium (for the same frequency).

Since the speed of light is maximum in vacuum, so the value of the refractive index of any medium (transparent media for visible light) is typically more than 1 in relation to vacuum; for X-rays it can be slightly less than 1.
The ability of a medium to refract light is also expressed in terms of its optical density.
A medium with higher refractive index (n) is called optically denser.
The speed of light is higher in a rarer medium than a denser medium.
Refraction of Light:
Light rays travel in a straight line in a homogeneous medium.

When a ray of light travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another with different refractive indices, its direction changes (This phenomenon is called refraction). At normal incidence, the direction does not change (though speed changes).
The ray approaching and striking the surface separating two media is called the incident ray.
The ray that travels in the second medium after refraction is called the refracted ray.
The point of incidence is the point where the incident ray strikes the interface/surface.
The normal is the line drawn perpendicular to the interface/ surface at the point of incidence.
The angle of incidence (i) is the angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle of refraction (r) is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal in the second medium.

When light goes from an optically rarer medium (lower refractive index) to an optically denser medium (higher refractive index) it bends towards the normal; from optically denser to optically rarer it bends away from the normal.

Examples of Refractive Phenomenon:
(i) An rod/pencil partially immersed in water appears bent/ displaced at the air-water interface when observed from outside.
(ii) A coin in water appears raised above its actual position.
(iii) Twinkling of stars (due to atmospheric refraction).
Refraction of light in a Prism:
A prism is a transparent refracting medium bounded by to non-parallel plane faces inclined at an angle (angle of prism).
Prisms are commonly made of glass (also other transparent materials are used).

In the above figure, the light ray AB, after falling on the first refracting surface PQ of the prism, is refracted along BC direction inside the prism, bending towards normal line EBF. Refracted ray BC at second refracting surface PR emerges into air along CD direction bending away from the normal line GCF. Thus, ABCD is the path of light in a Prism.
Dispersion of Light:
White light contains all visible wavelengths and is commonly represented as seven colours: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR).
The splitting/spreading of white light into its constituent colours (wavelengths) is called dispersion.
In spectrum violet color is at lower position and the red color is at the upper position.
In normal dispersion through a prism, red deviates least and violet deviates most.
In vacuum, all colours travel with the same speed.

In air and other media, speed is slightly less than in vacuum and depends on refractive index; because refractive index depends on wavelength, different colours have slightly different speeds (the effect is very small in air and larger in glass).
Thus the refractive index of any medium differs for different colors of light.
Speed of violet light is minimum and speed of red light is maximum in the glass.
In glass (normal dispersion), violet travels slower than red; hence refractive index is greatest for violet and least for red, so violet deviates most and red least.
Within the visible spectrum, violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency, while red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency.
Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection:
Critical angle (i(c)) is the angle of incidence beyond which rays of light passing through a denser medium to the surface of a rarer medium are no longer refracted but totally reflected.
In other words, critical angle (i(c)) is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°; for i > i(c), total internal reflection occurs.
Its value depends upon the nature of both mediums and color of rays.
For critical angle light must pass from a denser medium to rarer medium.
For glass-air surface the value of the critical angle is approximately 41.14º and for the water-air surface it is about 48.75º.

Reflection:
When light falls on the surface it may be absorbed, transmitted or reflected.
Reflection is when light bounces off an object.
Smooth, polished surfaces give specular (regular) reflection, while rough surfaces give diffuse reflection (reflected rays spread in many directions).
Silver is the better reflector of light.
Mirror:
A smooth well polished reflecting surface is called the mirror.
Mirrors are of two types–
(i) Plane Mirror
(ii) Spherical Mirror
Plane Mirror –
A plane mirror is a flat and smooth sheet of glass with a reflective metal layer (silver or aluminium) coated on the back surface and protected by paint.
The mirror used to see the face is a plane mirror.
Our face image formed in the plane mirror can not be obtained on screen, it can only be observed in the mirror.
So, the image formed in a plane mirror is an example of
virtual image
Such an image is also known as imaginary or unreal image.
The size of the image formed in the mirror is just equal to the size of the object.
The image and objects are at the same distance from the mirror at opposite sides.
The image is a laterally inverted mirror image of the object. If a person is reflected in a plane mirror, the image of his right hand appears to be the left hand of the image.
Spherical Mirror –
A spherical mirror is a mirror which has the shape of a piece cut out of a spherical surface.
These are of two types –
(i) Concave Mirror
(ii) Convex Mirror
Concave Mirror –
Concave mirrors have inwards curved reflecting surface.
Dentists use concave mirror for the examination of patient’s teeth producing big images of teeth.
Concave mirror are used as a reflector, for obtaining a sharp beam of light in torches, headlight of vehicles and searchlights.
Concave mirrors are also used for shaving to get clear image of face, etc.
Convex Mirror –
Convex mirrors have outward curved reflective surface.
It is used as rear-view side mirrors in vehicles.
Lens:
A lens is a transparent (usually homogeneous) material bounded by two surfaces, of which one or both are spherical; the other may be plane.
Curved surface may be spherical, cylindrical or elliptical, but these are mostly spherical.
Lens is of two types-
(i) Convex Lens
(ii) Concave Lens
Convex Lens –
Convex lens is thick in center but thin at corner.
Convex lens is also known as a converging lens because it converges the parallel light rays at one point. Its focal length is positive.

A convex (converging) lens forms a real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focus; if the object lies between the focus and the optical centre, the image is virtual, erect and enlarged (e.g., magnifying glass).
Convex lens is used to correct far-sightedness/ hypermetropia, an eye defect in which near objects are not clearly visible but long-distance objects are clearly visible.
Concave Lens –
Concave lens is thin at the centre but thick at the corner.
It is also known as a divergent lens because it diverges the parallel light rays. Its focal length is negative.
Objects appear smaller and farther through the concave lens and their images are virtual.
Concave lens is used to correct near-sightedness/ myopia, an eye defect in which far objects are not clearly visible but near objects are clearly visible.
Scattering:
Scattering is the redirection of light in many directions when it interacts with particles or inhomogeneities in a medium.
In many everyday cases (dust, smoke, fog, colloids), scattering can be understood as diffuse reflection of light by suspended particles.

The wavelength dependence of scattering depends on particle size: very fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) more effectively, while larger particles can scatter longer wavelengths and may make scattered light appear whitish.
The clear sky appears blue mainly because air molecules and other very fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than longer wavelengths.

Heat:
Heat is that energy which transfers from one system to another system as a result of their difference in temperature.
Its SI unit is joule (J).
Generally, calorie is also used as a unit (non-SI) of heat.
Temperature:
Temperature is a thermal state of an object, which indicates the degree of hotness/coldness of a body and determines the direction of heat flow.
Heat always transfer from a substance of higher temperature to a substance of lower temperature.
Measurement of temperature:
Thermometer is an instrument used for measuring the temperature.
To measure temperature, following temperature scales are commonly used –
(i) Celsius (Centigrade) Scale (°C):
A scale of temperature in which (at 1 atm) 0ºC represents the melting point of ice and 100ºC represents the boiling point of water.

Historically, the melting point of ice and boiling point of water (at 1 atm) were taken as fixed reference points close to 0°C and 100°C respectively (however they are very close, but not exactly equal in modern thermometry.
(ii) Kelvin Scale (K):
Kelvin is the absolute temperature scale.
On Kelvin Scale, ice melting point is 273.15K while the boiling point of water is 373.15K.
It is clear from above that 0ºC temperature on the Celsius scale is equal to 273.15 K (and 100°C is equal to 373.15 K) on the Kelvin scale.
So, temperature on Kelvin scale = temperature on Celsius scale + 273.15
(iii) Fahrenheit Scale (°F):
On this scale (at 1 atm) melting point of ice is 32ºF and boiling point of water is 212ºF is mentioned.

Temperature effects on matter:
On heating (at a given pressure), a solid may change to a liquid (melting), and a liquid may change to a gas (vaporisation/boiling).
On cooling, a gas may change to a liquid (condensation), and a liquid may change to a solid (freezing).
(i) Melting:
A process in which a solid converts into a liquid on heating.

The temperature at which solid matter melts and converts into a liquid at a given pressure (commonly quoted at atmospheric pressure) is known as its melting point. For example – ice melts at 0ºC into water. So, the melting point of ice is 0ºC.
Different solids have a different melting point. For example –
The melting point of ice – 0ºC The melting point of wax – ≈ 60ºC
The melting point of Iron – ≈ 1538ºC

The melting point of any solid shows the extent of the force of attraction between their particles (atoms or molecules). The high melting point of solid shows that it has a high force of attraction between particles.
(ii) Boiling:
Process in which a liquid converts into vapour throughout the bulk of the liquid on heating is known as boiling.
The temperature at which a liquid boils and converts into vapour very fastly at a given pressure (commonly at atmospheric pressure) is termed as its boiling point.
Different liquids have different boiling points.
For example (at 1 atm) –
(iii) Condensation:
The condensation process is the change of physical condition of matter from gas to liquid and it is the reverse phenomenon of vaporisation.
(iv) Freezing:
It is a phase transition in which a liquid turns into a solid when its temperature is lowered below its freezing point and this process is the reverse of melting.
On cooling a liquid, the temperature at which it turns into a solid is known as its freezing point.
The freezing point of water is about 0ºC.

For a pure substance at a given temperature the freezing point of the liquid and the melting point of solid is the same. For example – water freezes at 0ºC and ice melts at 0ºC i.e. both points are same.
Latent Heat:
During a change of state, heat is transferred without change in temperature.
Latent heat (for a process) is the amount of heat per unit mass transferred during change of state without temperature change.
Latent heat is mainly of two types –
(i) Latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing).
(ii) Latent heat of vaporisation (boiling/condensation).
Latent Heat of Fusion –
Required energy converting for solid into liquid phase or vice versa, is called latent heat of fusion. The value of latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ joule / kg (Jkg–¹).
Latent Heat of Vaporisation –
Required energy converting for liquid into vapour is called latent heat of vaporisation. The value of latent heat of vaporisation of water (at 100°C, 1 atm) is 22.6 × 10⁵ joule / kg (Jkg–¹).

When water turns into vapour, it absorbs the latent heat. By experiments, it has been observed that burning from steam is more severe than burning from boiling water, although both are at the same temperature i.e. at 100ºC.

Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water at the same temperature because when steam condenses on the skin, it releases its latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat released as the condensed water cools.
Steam at 100°C carries 22.6 × 10⁵ joule/kg more heat than water at 100°C.
Sublimation:

On heating when a solid changes directly into gas (without becoming liquid), then that phenomenon is known as sublimation. Direct change from gas to solid (without becoming liquid) is called deposition.
Some substances having the sublimation property are Ammonium chloride, Iodine, Camphor and Naphthalene, etc.
Evaporation:
The process in which liquid turns into vapours below its boiling point is termed as evaporation. It may occur at room temperature.
Wet clothes dry due to evaporation of water.
Pond water dries up due to evaporation of water.
Increase in temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
Evaporation increases with temperature; at the boiling point, vaporisation becomes boiling (bulk phenomenon).
In case of low humidity in the air, the evaporation rate is high and water evaporates very soon, while higher humidity in the air, results into a low rate of evaporation.
Cooling by Evaporation:
When a liquid evaporates, it absorbs heat (latent heat) from its surroundings, producing cooling.
A good example of cooling by evaporation is cooling of earthen pots.

The earthen pot has many tiny pores in its wall. The water diffuses out from the pores and evaporates continuously. The required heat for evaporation is taken from the water itself, it leads to a lowering of temperature in the remaining amount of water.
The sweating process is more in the summer season. Evaporation of sweat provides cooling to our body as it absorbs heat from the skin.
Cotton clothes are the best absorbent of water. They absorb the sweat of our body and expose it for easier evaporation.

Synthetic clothes such as polyesters are unable to absorb sweat in excess quantity, so these are unable to provide cooling to our body. Due to this reason, cotton clothes are given priority in the summer season.
A fan increases evaporation of sweat, so we feel the cooling.
In desert room cooler, the cooling effect is produced due to evaporation of water. It cools better in hot and dry days because higher temperature and lower humidity increase the rate of evaporation.

Wave:

Wave involves the transfer of energy without net transfer of matter. A wave can be described as a disturbance that travels through a material medium or through vacuum/ space (depending on the type of wave), transferring energy from one location (its source) to another location without net transfer of matter.
In classical physics, waves are often grouped into two major types:
1. Mechanical waves (require a material medium).
2. Electromagnetic waves (do not require a material medium).
Additionally matter waves or de Broglie waves exist in quantum physics. These waves are associated with the moving particles.
Mechanical Waves:
A mechanical wave is a wave in which particles of a material medium oscillate about their mean positions and energy is transmitted through the medium.
The medium as a whole does not move with the wave; only oscillations and energy transfer propagate.
Mechanical waves transfer energy which propagates in the same direction as the wave.
Mechanical waves can be produced only in media which possess elasticity (restoring force) and inertia.
Types of mechanical waves –
During transmission of a mechanical wave through a medium, the medium particles start to vibrate. On the basis of the direction of particle vibration, mechanical waves are of two types –
(i) Transverse waves
(ii) Longitudinal waves
(i) Transverse Waves:
Atransverse wave is a travelling wave in which the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular (right angled) to the direction of energy transfer (wave propagation).
Examples –

a. Vibration on a stretched string/rope: When one end of the rope is bound with hook and another free end is vibrating upward and downward, the produced vibration in rope particle is perpendicular to the wave direction.
b. Waves in solids (e.g., shear waves in solids).
Transverse mechanical waves propagate in solids (which can sustain shear stress) and do not propagate in fluids (liquids and gases) as bulk shear waves.

Surface water waves are special: particle motion has both vertical and horizontal components; ocean waves are a combination of longitudinal and transverse motions, and oscillations can extend below the surface with decreasing amplitude.
Electromagnetic waves such as light are also transverse waves.

In transverse wave, maximum displacement in upward side (highest point) from the equilibrium state is termed as 'crest' while maximum displacement in the downward side (lowest point) is termed as 'trough'. The crest is the top of the wave and trough is the bottom.
The distance between two consecutive crests or two consequitive troughs is the 'wavelength'.
Wavelength is represented by Greek letter 'λ' (lambda).
(ii) Longitudinal Waves:
A longitudinal wave is a travelling wave in which particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Sound waves in air (and in fluids generally) are the standard example of a longitudinal wave.
Waves produced in a spring (slinky) when pushed/pulled along its length.
In a longitudinal wave, regions where particle/coils are closer together are called 'compressions', while regions where particles/coils are farther apart are called 'rarefactions'.
The distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions is 'wavelength' (λ).
Direction of wave progation
Longitudinal waves are originated in all mediums i.e. solid, liquid & gas.
Along with propagating transverse waves on the surface of the liquid, longitudinal waves can be propagated inside the liquid.
Longitudinal waves are always mechanical waves.
Time Period:
In case of a wave propagating in a medium, time taken by the particle for one complete oscillation (one vibration) is known as the time period of the wave. It is denoted by 'T'.
Increase in frequency of waves, results into a decrease of time period.
Frequency:

During propagation of the wave in the medium, frequency is the number of occurrences of repeating event per unit of time by particle. In other words, the frequency is the number of oscillations per second.

Sound:
Sound is a mechanical disturbance (pressure wave) in a material medium that produces the sensation of hearing.
Sound travels in the form of waves.
Vibrating objects/matters produce sound.
The substance through which sound travels is called a medium.
Sound waves are mechanical waves.
A medium (solid, liquid, gas, etc.) is necessary for their propagation; sound does not propagate in vacuum.
Sound is transmitted through gases, plasma, and liquids as longitudinal waves. Through solids, however, it can be transmitted as longitudinal as well as transverse (shear) waves.
Speed of Sound:
Speed of sound depends upon the nature/properties of the medium through which it propagates.
Speed of sound varies in different media.
Sound propagates slowest in gases.
Sound propagates faster than gases in liquids.
Speed of sound is fastest in solids.
Sound does not propagate in vacuum.
Speed of sound in steel is about 17 times to speed of sound in air.
Speed of sound depends upon temperature in air.
Increase in temperature results to increase in the speed of sound (in summer season the speed of sound is more than that of winter season).
Humidity of air plays a very important role in the speed of sound.
Speed of sound in humid air is more than that of dry air.
Speed of sound in different mediums
Frequency range of Sound:
Sound waves have been classified into three types on the basis of their frequency range. These are as follows:
(i) Audible sound Waves:
Our ear is only capable to hear such sound waves.

Electric Conductivity:
Within the atom, electrons nearest to the nucleus are strongly bound to the positively charged nucleus (due to protons) by electrostatic attraction.
Electrons farther from the nucleus (outer/valence electrons) are comparatively less tightly bound.
Because they are less tightly bound, such outer electrons can be removed more easily (with sufficient external energy).
In metals, some outer electrons become delocalized in the solid and act as ‘conduction (free) electrons’.
Free (conduction) electrons are electrons not bound to a particular atom and are free to move through the material when an external electric field is applied.
In general physics, a free electron is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom or molecule.
Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering) show high electrical conductivity.
Silver has the highest electrical conductivity among common metals at room temperature; copper, gold, and aluminium are also good conductors.
Electrical conduction is also found in some liquids (e.g., electrolytes) and in gases when the gas becomes ionized (plasma/discharge).

In metals, conduction is mainly due to the motion of electrons. In electrolytic liquids, conduction is mainly due to the motion of positive and negative ions. In ionized gases, conduction occurs due to electrons and ions.

Gases are generally poor conductors under ordinary conditions, but they conduct when sufficiently ionized. Gas breakdown/discharge depends on the electric field and on conditions such as the pressure-gap product (Paschen-type behaviour); electrical discharges/arcs can occur even at atmospheric pressure (e.g., lightning, arc lamps/welding).
Non-conductor:
Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.
Under sufficiently strong electric fields, an insulator may conduct due to dielectric breakdown.
Semiconductor:
Asemiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators.
Its conductivity can increase due to temperature (thermal generation of charge carriers) and due to controlled impurity addition (doping).
Adding controlled impurities to a semiconductor is called doping; doped semiconductors are called extrinsic semiconductors.
Semiconductors typically show decreasing resistance with increasing temperature, opposite to most metals.
Examples: Silicon, Germanium, Selenium, Tellurium (and α-Tin as a special elemental case).

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) is a multilateral treaty that bans nuclear weapons test explosions and any other nuclear explosions, for both civilian and military purposes, in all environments.

It was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 September 1996, but has not entered into force. The ratifications of nine specific nations are still required for the Treaty to enter into force.

Of the 44 States included in Annex 2 (of the Treaty) required for entry into force of the CTBT, all have signed with the exceptions of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK-North Korea), India, and Pakistan. National Supercomputing Mission (NSM):
The National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) is a flagship initiative by the Government of India to empower the country with high-performance computing (HPC) capabilities.

Launched in 2015, the mission aims to enhance India’s technological prowess in supercomputing, foster research and development (R&D), and support scientific advancements across academia, industry, and government sectors.

NSM was set up to provide the country with supercomputing infrastructure to meet the increasing computational demands of academia, researchers, MSMEs, and startups. It is a first of its kind attempt to boost the country’s computing power.

The Mission envisages empowering our national academic and R&D institutions spread over the country by installing supercomputers of various capacities. Access to these supercomputers is provided through the National Knowledge Network (NKN). The NKN is another program of the government which connects academic institutions and R&D labs over a high-speed network.
Academic and R&D institutions as well as key user departments/ministries would participate by using these facilities and develop applications of national relevance.

The Mission also includes development of highly professional High-Performance Computing (HPC) aware human resource for meeting challenges of development of these applications. HRD activities in this area are steered through five training centres at Pune, Kharagpur, Chennai, Palakkad, and Goa to expand the awareness and familiarization of supercomputing with college students and researchers.

Under NSM, as of 30 November, 2025, a total of 37 supercomputers with cumulative compute capacity of 39 Petaflops, have been deployed across various academic institutions, research organizations, and R&D labs, including prominent institutions like IISc, IITs, C-DAC, and other institutions from Tier-II and Tier III cities of the country under NSM.

The supercomputing systems commissioned under NSM have achieved an overall utilization rate of over 85%, with many systems exceeding 95%, demonstrating a high level of usage and efficiency in their computational capacity.

NSM is steered jointly by Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and implemented by Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru.
