This type of memory is non-volatile.
The information remains stored even after the computer is switched off; it is not deleted.
'Basic input & output system' (BIOS)/ Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware is stored in system flash memory (EEPROM/flash) and can be updated.
External Memory or Secondary Memory:
Main examples of secondary memory are–
(i) Hard Disk
(ii) Floppy Disk
(iii) CD ROM
(iv) DVD
(v) Pen Drive
(vi) Blu-ray Disc.
Hard Disk –
A hard disk has one or more platters/disks. Each disk is divided into the track and each track is divided into the sector.
DVD (Digital Versatile Disc or Digital Video Disc) -
It is an optical storage device, which is similar to CD, but its storage capacity is much more than that of CD.
Its capacity depends on DVD type; commonly about 4.7 GB vs about 650 MB for a CD –about 7 times; and higher for double layer/double sided DVDs.
DVD formats include DVD-ROM/DVD-Video (read only), DVD-R and DVD+R (record-once), DVD-RW and DVD+RW (rewritable), and DVD-RAM (rewritable).
Pen Drive –
Pen Drive is also known as a
USB flash drive
. It is widely used as a portable data storage device.
Blu-ray Disc –
Blu-ray Disc is an optical disc, which is the advance version of DVD. In Blu-ray Disc, blue represents the colour of laser and ray represents optical ray.
Input Units:
Such devices which are used to enter data and instructions in the computer are known as Input Units.
Examples of input devices are – keyboard, mouse, scanner, trackball, and lightpen, etc.
Output Unit:
An output device is any device used to send data from a computer to another device or user.
Examples of output units are – printer, speakers, headphones, projectors, monitors, plotter, and LCD, etc.
Output can be visual (monitor/projector), audio (speakers/ headphones), and hardcopy (printer/plotter), etc.
Computer Software:
Computer software has been divided into two parts –
1. System software
2. Application software
System Software:
System software is used for operating computer system. They are designed to provide a platform for other software.
Examples of system software include operating systems like Microsoft Windows, macOS, Ubuntu/Linux, and Android (in smartphones and tablets).
It controls the internal operations of the computer.
Application Software:
Application software is used by the user to perform specific task.
These are installed according to user's requirements.
There are different application software for different required applications such as, for writing, to keep data, to record the song, calculation of salary and accounts of transactions.
Application software include such things as database programs, word processors, Web browsers, spreadsheets, graphic software, computational science software, game engines, industrial automation, etc.
Computer Programming Languages:

For functioning, the computer follows the instructions given by the programmer. This set of instructions is called a (computer) program that produces various kinds of output. A program is written in a programming language.
Generations of Computer Languages:
Programming languages are often classified into ‘generations’as a broad taxonomy (however, the boundaries are not universally fixed). A common classification is:

machine language (1GL), assembly language (2GL), high level languages (3GL), very high-level/nonprocedural languages and tools often used for database/query reporting and application generation (4GL), and logic constraint-based AI-oriented languages sometimes labeled as 5GL.
First-Generation Languages (1GL):
Machine Language:
The most basic form, consisting of binary code (0s and 1s) that the CPU directly executes. Examples: Machine code specific to a particular computer architecture.
Characteristics:
Very difficult for humans to read/write; hardware-dependent, requiring direct interaction with the computer's hardware.
Second-Generation Languages (2GL):
Assembly Language:
Uses mnemonics and symbolic names that map closely to machine instructions and is translated by an assembler. Examples: Assembly language specific to a particular CPU architecture.
Characteristics:
Still low-leveland hardware-dependent; requiring knowledge of the underlying hardware, but easier to program than machine language.
Third-Generation Languages (3GL):
High-Level Languages:
More human-readable; typically compiled or interpreted into machine code.Examples: C, C++, Java, Python, PHP, Perl, C#, BASIC, Pascal, Fortran, ALGOL, COBOL, etc.
Characteristics:
More portable and maintainable than low-level languages.
Fourth-Generation Languages (4GL):
Very High-Level / Largely Nonprocedural Languages and Tools:

Often used for database querying, reporting, and rapid application development where users specify what result is needed rather than how to compute it. These languages are designed to simplify database management and scripting tasks, often using declarative syntax. Examples: SQL; query-by-example (QBE); report generators and application generators (tooling category).
Characteristics:
Focus on what needs to be done rather than how, making them more efficient for specific tasks.
Fifth-Generation Languages (5GL):
Logic/Constraint-Based AI-Oriented Languages:
Often associated with logic programming and AI research; sometimes also defined by natural language understanding and processing. Examples: Prolog, OPS5, Mercury, etc.
Characteristics:
Emphasize logic/rules/constraints and knowledge representation approaches for problem solving, allowing computers to solve problems in a more human like way.
Computer Network:
A computer network is a set of computers/nodes with supporting network links connected together for the purpose of communicating/exchanging data and sharing resources.
Types of Network:
Following are the types of network-
(i) Local Area Network (LAN):
A local area network is a computer network that interconnects computers and other devices within a limited area such as a residence, school, laboratory, university campus/building or office.
(ii) Wide Area Network (WAN):

A wide Area Network is a telecommunications network or computer network that extends over a large geographical area (e.g., across cities/ countries/continents). WAN connectivity is often provided using telecommunications infrastructure, including leased circuits and carrier networks.
(iii) Metropolitan Area Network (MAN):
A high-speed network spanning a metropolitan area (typically a large city) and commonly used to interconnect multiple LANs across that area using high-speed links and networking equipment.
World Wide Web (www):
The World Wide Web (WWW) is an information space of interrelated resources identified by URIs/URLs and accessed over the Internet using web technologies (commonly HTTP- Hyper Text Transfer Protocol).

Commonly known as 'the Web', it is an information system on the Internet which allows documents and other web resources to be connected to other documents/resources by hypertext links, enabling the user to search (navigate/ browse) for information by moving from one document to another.
British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the Web in 1989. He wrote the first web browser while employed at CERN near Geneva, Switzerland.

Web resources are commonly represented using HTML (Hyper Text Markup Language) and delivered by web servers to user agents (e.g., web browsers), which render text and link to or embed media such as images, audio, and video.
E-mail:
E-mail (electronic mail) is a method of exchanging digital messages over computer networks (today, primarily the Internet).

Raymond (Ray) Tomlinson is widely known for inventing network electronic mail and introducing the “@” convention for addressing; however, earlier email-like systems existed on time-sharing computers (e.g., CTSS in the 1960s).
Email first entered limited use in early time-sharing systems and later became a major application on computer networks; today it operates primarily over the Internet.
Question Bank
Notes
Sputnik-1:
It was the first artificial Earth satellite.
It was launched into space in an elliptical low Earth orbit (LEO) by Soviet Union on 4 October, 1957.
It was an important incident in the history of space science.
About 98 minutes were taken by this satellite to revolve one round of Earth.
It was in orbit for three weeks before its batteries died, then silently revolved for two more months before fell back and burned into the Earth's atmosphere.
It revolved around the Earth for 92 days and completed 1440 rounds of Earth.
Sputnik-2:
It was the second artificial Earth satellite launched by the Soviet Union.
It was launched into Earth orbit on 3 November, 1957.
It was the first spacecraft to carry a living animal into Earth orbit, a Soviet space dog named
Laika
, who died a few hours after the launch.
Vostok-I:
It was the first spaceflight of the Vostok programme and the first manned spaceflight in history.
It was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome on April 12, 1961 with Soviet cosmonaut
Yuri Gagarin
, making him the first human to reach into outer space.
He returned to Earth after successful completion of one round of Earth.
Gagarin was weightless for 89 minutes (in-orbit time) of his 108 minutes of total flight time.
First Landing on Moon:
A Moon landing is the arrival of a spacecraft on the surface of Moon.
This includes both unmanned & manned missions.
The first human made object to reach the surface of the Moon was the Soviet Union's
Luna 2
mission, on 13 September, 1959 (as dated by NASA).
The man reached on Moon under Apollo program of U.S.A.
Apollo Program crewed missions were started with Apollo-7 (1968) and ended with Apollo-17 (1972).
Apollo-11
was the spaceflight that landed the first two people on the Moon.
Mission commander
Neil Armstrong
and pilot
Buzz Aldrin,
both American landed the lunar module Eagle on July 20, 1969 and walked on the lunar surface.
Michael Collins
piloted the command module Columbia alone in lunar orbit.
Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 hours, 36 minutes on the lunar surface.
Launch Vehicles of India:

The Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3) was a project started in the early 1970s by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to develop the technology needed to launch satellites. The project was headed by APJ Abdul Kalam. SLV was intended to reach a height of400 km and carry a payload of 40 kg.
(i) Satellite Launch Vehicle-3 (SLV-3):
It was India's first experimental satellite launch vehicle.
It was an all solid, four stage vehicle weighing 17 tonnes with a height of 22m.
It was capable of placing about 40 kg. class payloads in LEO (Low Earth Orbit).

It was successfully launched on July 18, 1980 from Sriharikota Range (SHAR), when Rohini Satellite, RS-1 was placed in orbit (The space centre, which was popularly known as SHAR (Sriharikota Range) was renamed as Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR on September 5, 2002).
India became the sixth member of an exclusive club of space-faring nations with this achievement.
RS-D1 was launched by SLV-3 from SHAR center on 31 May, 1981 and RS-D2 was launched on 17 April, 1983.
(ii) Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV):
It was a five stage, all solid-fuel rocket. It was developed by the ISRO.
It was capable to place 150 kg satellite into a 400 km circular orbit (in LEO).
Its height was 24 metres and lift offweight was 40 tonnes.

Its first developmental flight took place on 24 March, 1987 and the second on 13 July, 1988. The third developmental flight, ASLV-D3 was launched on 20 May, 1992, when SROSS-C was put into orbit. ASLV-D4 launched on 4 May, 1994, orbited SROSS-C2.
After that, the SLV-3 and ASLV launchers have been retired by ISRO.
(iii) Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV):
The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is an expendable (used only once) medium-lift launch vehicle.
It was designed and operated by the ISRO.
It is 44 metre long with a mass 295 tonnes.
It is four stage third generation launch vehicle of India. It is the first Indian launch vehicle to be equipped with liquid stages.
In first and third stage it uses solid propellants while in 2nd & 4th stage liquid propellants are used.
Propellants have two parts-
(a) Fuel - in which combustion takes place.
(b) Oxidiser - It assists in combustion of fuel (Provides oxygen for combustion).
Six boosters are attached with first stage of rocket. These are filled with solid propellants. The propellants amount is adjusted according to the requirements.
Hydroxyl Terminated Polybutadine (HTBP) is used as solid propellant in core motor of first stage and attached boosters with it.
The second stage of PSLV is operated by liquid propellant in which unsymmetrical Dimethyl Hydrazine-UDMH is used as fuel and N₂O₄ (Nitrogen Tetra Oxide) is used as oxidiser.
The third stage is operated by solid propellant. HTBP is used in this stage.
In the 4th & last stage as liquid propellant - Monomethyl Hydrozine (MMH) and as an oxydiser - mixed oxides of Nitrogen (MON-3) is used.
The first mission of PSLV-D1 (20 September, 1993) was unsuccessful. After its first successful launch on 15 Oct. 1994 (PSLV-D2), PSLV emerged as the reliable and versatile '
workhorse
' launch vehicle of India with 64 missions (in which 61 are successful) till January, 2026.

Most notable among these was the launch of PSLV-C37 on 15 February 2017, successfully deploying 104 satellites in sun-synchronous orbit, which was a record for the highest number of satellites sent to space on a single launch, until 24 January 2021, when SpaceX launched the Transporter-1 mission on a Falcon 9 rocket carrying 143 satellites into orbit.

This vehicle successfully launched two spacecrafts (both with XL version) – Chandrayaan-1 in 2008 and Mars Orbiter Spacecraft (Mangalyaan) in 2013 – that later traveled to Moon and Mars respectively. PSLV also launched India's first space observatory, Astrosat and India's first solar mission, Aditya-L1.
Core Alone is PSLV lightest version without six strap-on motors (boosters). It is used for launching smaller payloads
i.e. 500-700 kg payload satellites.
The boosters attached with first stage of rocket are used when satellites with approximate payload of 1500 kg are launched. This version is known as
standard version
. It can take upto 1,750 kg of payload to Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbits of 600 km altitude.
In its boosters nine tonne solid propellant is used.
PSLV-XL
(PSLV-extra large; Lift off mass - 320 tonnes) is an extended version of PSLV. In its boosters twelve tonne propellant is used. It was first used to launch Chandrayaan-I in its orbit.
PSLV-DL
is another variant of PSLV (with two strap-on motors), which was first launched on 24 January, 2019.
Latest variant of this vehicle is
PSLV-QL
(with four Strap on motors) which was first launched on 1 April, 2019.

Due to its unmatched reliability, PSLV has also been used (generally in XL version) to launch various satellites into Geosynchronous and Geostationary Orbits, like satellites from the IRNSS constellation.
At present, PSLV is configured with four variants like 6, 4, 2 solid rocket strap-on motors and core alone versions. Variants will be chosen based on the payload weights and orbit to be accomplished.
(iv) Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV):
Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is an expendable launch system operated by ISRO.
PSLV can carry up to 1425 kg of payload to Sub Geostationary Transfer Orbits (Sub-GTO).
So, India has developed more powerful rockets (i.e. GSLV/ LVM3) to launch massive payloads satellites to GTO.
Current official launcher capabilities (ISRO/NSIL):
(a) GSLV (Mk II): Payload to GTO is 2,250 kg.
(b) LVM3 (earlier referred to as GSLV Mk III): Payload to GTO is 4,000 kg; payload to LEO (600 km) is 8,000 kg.

GSLV-MkII is a three stage vehicle with four liquid strap ons. Its height is 51.73m (with Ogive PLF) with lift-off mass 420 tonnes. The indigenously developed Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS) forms third stage of GSLV-MkII.

GSLV-MkIII (now renamed as LVM3) is a three stage heavy lift launch vehicle which has two solid strap-ons, a core liquid booster and a CUS. Its height and lift-offmass are 43.5 m and 640 tonnes, respectively. It is designed to carry 4-tonne class satellites into GTO and 8000 kg of payload to LEO of 600 km altitude, which is about twice the capability of GSLV Mk II.
Chandrayaan-2 was launched on its mission to the Moon from Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota on 22 July, 2019 by GSLV-Mk III (LVM3-M1).

The first commercial mission of GSLV-Mark III (LVM3-M2) was successfully launched on 23 October, 2022 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. This was the fifth flight of LVM3. A total of 36 One Web Gen-1 satellites of about 150 kg each totalling about 5796 kg were launched to a circular low-Earth orbit (LEO) of about 601 km in this mission. It was the first launch of LVM3 to LEO and the first Indian rocket with a six-tonne payload class.
Chandrayaan-3 was launched on its mission to the Moon from SDSC, SHAR, Sriharikota on 14 July, 2023 by LVM3-M4.
GSLV-MkIII (now renamed as LVM3) is also known as
fatboy
Previously scientists have named PSLV as
workhorse
and GSLV-II as
naughty boy
(v) Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV)
SSLV is being developed with complete indigenous technologies to meet the small satellite launch market on demand driven basis.
It is a 3-stage launch vehicle configured with three solid propulsion stages and liquid propulsion based Velocity Trimming Module (VTM) as a terminal stage.

SSLV is 2m in diameter and 34 min length with lift off weight of ~ 120 tonnes. It is capable of launching ~ 500 kg satellite in 500 km low-Earth orbit (LEO) or ~ 300 kg satellite in 500 km Sun-synchronous orbit.
The key features of SSLV are low cost, with low turn around time, flexibility in accommodating multiple satellites, launch on demand feasibility, minimal launch infrastructure requirements etc.

The first developmental flight of this launch vehicle (SSLV-D1), carrying a Earth Observation Satellite (EOS 02) and a student-made satellite AzaadiSAT was launched on 7 August, 2022 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota. However, SSLV-D1 placed these satellites into an elliptical orbit instead of a circular one, so they were no longer usable.

The second developmental flight of this launch vehicle (SSLV-D2) was launched successfully on 10 February, 2023 from SDSC SHAR, Sriharikota. It injected EOS 07 (a 156.3 kg Earth Observation Satellite of ISRO), Janus-1 (a 10.2 kg satellite belongs to ANTARIS, USA) and AzaadiSAT-2 (a 8.7 kg satellite which is a combined effort of about 750 girl students across India guided by Space Kidz India, Chennai) into 450 km circular LEO.

The third developmental flight of this launch vehicle (SSLV-D3) was launched successfully on 16 August, 2024, from SDSC SHAR, Sriharikota. The SSLV-D3 placed EOS-8 (a 175.5 kg Earth Observation Satellite of ISRO) precisely into the 475 km circular LEO. The mission also carried SR-0 DEMOSAT passenger satellite. This flight completed the SSLV Development Project and enables operational missions by Indian industry and
New Space India Limited (NSIL)
ISRO is developing a new dedicated launch site in
Kulasekharapattinam
, a coastal village in Thoothukudi district of Tamil Nadu, which will handle SSLV launches. PM Narendra Modi remotely laid the foundation stone for India's this second spaceport on 28 February, 2024.
Vikram-S:

Vikram-S, India’s first privately built rocket, was accomplished successfully as a suborbital test flight on 18 November 2022 by M/s Skyroot Aerospace Pvt. Ltd., Hyderabad, from the sounding rocket launch complex at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. The mission for the rocket launch was named as 'Prarambh', meaning beginning.
As a tribute, the rocket was named after Vikram Sarabhai, who is considered as father of India's space programme.
Vikram-S rocket was developed by Skyroot Aerospace and the mission was authorized by IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre).
Cryogenics:
In physics, cryogenics deals with the production of very low temperatures and the behaviour/effects of materials at those temperatures.

Although the boundary can vary by context, cryogenics has generally been used to refer to temperatures below about –150°C, and the cryogenic region is often considered below about 120 K (about –153°C).
A person who works in the field of cryogenics is called a cryogenicist.
The word originates from the Greek words kryos meaning ‘frost’ and genic meaning ‘to produce.’
Prof. Kamerlingh Onnes (Leiden University) used the word in 1894 in the context of producing much lower temperatures and the liquefaction of permanent gases.
Normal boiling points (at 1 atm) of some cryogenic fluids:

Cryogenics has many applications (industrial, medical, research, etc.). In rocketry, cryogenics is used for cryogenic propellants, where fuels/oxidisers may be stored as liquids to reduce volume and mass.
In cryogenic rocket engines, liquid hydrogen (fuel) and liquid oxygen (oxidiser) are commonly used.
Ramjet:
A ramjet is sometimes referred to as a 'flying stovepipe' or an athodyd (an abbreviation of aero-thermodynamic duct).
It is a form of air-breathingjet engine, that uses the engine's forward motion to compress incoming air without an axial or centrifugal compressor.
Ramjets work best at speeds of Mach 2 and higher; typically operate effectively around Mach 3 to Mach 5 (design-dependent).
Scramjet:
A scramjet is also known as Supersonic Combustion Ramjet in which combustion takes place in supersonic airflow.

Like a ramjet, a scramjet relies on high vehicle speed to compress the incoming air, but whereas a ramjet decelerates the air to subsonic velocities before combustion, the airflow in a scramjet is supersonic throughout the entire engine. That allows the scramjet to operate efficiently at extremely high speeds.
Scramjets are designed for speeds beyond Mach 6.
In Scramjet engine developed by ISRO, Hydrogen is used as fuel and Oxygen is used from the atmosphere as the oxidizer.

The first experimental mission of ISRO's Scramjet engine towards the realisation of an Air Breathing Propulsion System was successfully conducted on 28 August, 2016 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) SHAR, Sriharikota. This test was the maiden short duration experimental test of ISRO's Scramjet engine with a hypersonic flight at Mach 6. ISRO's Advanced Technology Vehicle (ATV), which is an advanced sounding rocket, was the solid rocket booster used for the test of Scramjet engine at supersonic conditions.
Reusable Launch Vehicle - Technology Demonstrator (RLV-T.D.):
It is one of the most technologically challenging endeavors of ISRO towards developing essential technologies for a fully reusable launch vehicle to enable low cost access to space.

The configuration of RLV-TD is similar to that of an aircraft and combines the complexity of both launch vehicles and aircraft. The winged RLV-TD has been configured to act as a flying test bed to evaluate various technologies, namely, hypersonic flight, autonomous landing and powered cruise flight. In future, this vehicle will be scaled up to become the first stage of India's reusable two stage orbital launch vehicle.

RLV-TD was successfully flight tested on 23 May, 2016 from SDSC SHAR, Sriharikota validating the critical technologies such as autonomous navigation, guidance & control, reusable thermal protection system and re-entry mission management.
Sounding Rocket:
A sounding Rocket, sometimes called a research rocket, is an instrument-carrying rocket designed to take measurements and perform scientific experiments during its sub-orbital flight.

Sounding rockets can carry research payloads to high altitudes; ISRO’s operational Rohini sounding rockets cover an apogee range of about 80–475 km (globally, some multi-stage sounding rockets can reach much higher altitudes).
Hubble Space Telescope:
The Hubble Space Telescope (often referred to as HST or Hubble) is a space telescope that was launched into low Earth orbit in 1990 and remains in operation.
The Hubble telescope is named after astronomer Edwin Hubble and is one of NASA's Great Observatories, along with the
Compton Gamma Ray Observatory
Chandra X-ray Observatory
(1999-present), and the
Spitzer Space Telescope

The telescope completed 36 years of operation in April, 2026 and is not expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere until the mid-2030s at the earliest; expected to remain operational into the next decade.
Compton Gamma Ray Observatory (CGRO):
It was a space observatory detecting photons with energies spanning roughly 20-30 keV to 30 GeV (depending on definition/instrument used), in Earth orbit from 1991 to 2000.
The observatory was launched from Space Shuttle Atlantis during STS-37 on April 5, 1991, and operated until its deorbit on June 4, 2000.
Chandra X-ray Observatory:

The Chandra X-ray Observatory (CXO), previously known as the Advanced X-ray Astrophysics Facility (AXAF), is a Flagship-class space telescope launched aboard the Space Shuttle Columbia during STS-93 by NASA on July 23, 1999.
Chandra is an Earth Satellite in a 64-hour orbit, and its mission is ongoing as of 2026.
The telescope is named after the Nobel Prize-winning Indian-American astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
Spitzer Space Telescope:
Formerly it was known as Space Infrared Telescope Facility.
It was launched on 25 August, 2003 by Delta II Heavy Rocket from Cape Canaveral and retired on 30 January, 2020.
It was the fourth and final of the NASA's
Great Observatories
programme.
Each observatory of this programme has been launched into space for surveying the different radiations as ultraviolet/visible, gamma, X-ray & infrared.
Their main purpose is to study the early universe, young galaxies and forming stars and is used to detect dust disks around stars, considered an important signpost of planetary formation.
Kepler Space Telescope:
The Kepler space telescope was launched by NASA on Delta II rocket in 2009 to discover Earth-sized planets orbiting other stars (exoplanets).
Named after astronomer Johannes Kepler, the spacecraft was launched into an Earth-trailing heliocentric orbit.

After nine and a half years of operation, the telescope's reaction control system fuel was depleted, and NASA announced its retirement on October 30, 2018. Kepler observed more than 530,500 stars and detected more than 2,600 exoplanets.
TESS:

Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) is a space telescope for NASA's Explorer program, designed to search for exoplanets using the transit method in an area 400 times larger than that covered by the Kepler mission.
It was launched on 18 April 2018, atop a Falcon 9 launch vehicle.
ASTROSAT:
ASTROSAT is India's first dedicated multi-wavelength space observatory. It was launched on a PSLV-XL on 28 September, 2015.

This scientific satellite mission endeavours for a more detailed understanding of our universe. One of the unique features of ASTROSAT mission is that enables the simultaneous multi-wavelength observations of various astronomical objects with a single satellite.

ASTROSAT observes universe in the optical, Ultraviolet, low and high energy X-ray regions of the electromagnetic spectrum, whereas most other scientific satellites are capable of observing a narrow range of wavelength band.

Multi-wavelength observations of ASTROSAT can be further extended with co-ordinated observations using other spacecraft and ground based observations. All major astronomy institutions and some universities in India are participating in these observations.
XPoSat:

XPoSat (X-ray Polarimeter Satellite) is the first dedicated scientific satellite from ISRO to carry out research in space-based polarisation measurements of X-ray emission from celestial sources. ISRO's PSLV-C58 has launched XPoSat Satellite on 1 January, 2024.

The spacecraft carried two scientific payloads in a low Earth orbit. The primary payload POLIX (Polarimeter Instrument in X-rays) will measure the polarimetry parameters (degree and angle of polarization) in medium X-ray energy range of 8-30 keV photons of astronomical origin. The XSPECT (X-ray Spectroscopy and Timing) payload will give spectroscopic information in the energy range of 0.8-15 keV.
POLIX is realized by Raman Research Institute and XSPECT is by Space Astronomy Group of URSC.
James Webb Space Telescope:

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is developed by NASA in collaboration with the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). It is designed primarily to conduct infrared astronomy.
The JWST was launched on 25 December, 2021 from Kourou, French Guiana with ESA's Ariane 5 rocket.
It is intended to succeed the Hubble Space Telescope as NASA's flagship mission in astrophysics.
It is named after James E.Webb, who was the administrator of NASA from 1961 to 1968.
In July, 2022, JWST's commissioning process was complete.
On 12 July, 2022 NASA released the full-color images and marked the official beginning of Webb's science mission.
International Space Station:

The International Space Station (ISS) is a large space station assembled and maintained in low-Earth orbit by a collaboration of five space agencies: NASA (United States), Roscosmos (Russia), JAXA (Japan), ESA (Europe), CSA (Canada), and their contractors. ISS is the largest space station ever built.

Its primary purpose is performing microgravity and space environment experiments. Operationally the station is divided into two sections: the Russian Orbital Segment assembled by Roscosmos and the US Orbital Segment assembled by NASA, JAXA, ESA and CSA.
The ISS maintains an orbit with an average altitude of 400 kilometres (250 mi) and circles the Earth in roughly 93 minutes, completing 15.5 orbits per day.

The ISS programme combines two prior plans to construct crewed Earth-orbiting stations: Space Station Freedom planned by the United States, and the Mir-2 station planned by the Soviet Union. The first ISS module was launched in 1998. Major modules have been launched by Proton and Soyuz rockets and by the Space Shuttle launch system.
The first long-term residents, Expedition 1, arrived on 2 November, 2000. As of March, 2026, 292 individuals from 26 countries have visited this space station.
Tiangong Space Station:

Tiangong space station is a permanently crewed space station constructed by China and operated by China Manned Space Agency. Tiangong is a modular design, with modules docked together while in low- Earth orbit, between 340 and 450 km (210 and 280 mi) above the surface.
It is China's first long-term space station, part of the Tiangong program and the core of the 'Third Step' of the China Manned Space Program.
The space station aims to provide opportunities for space based experiments and a platform for building capacity for scientific and technological innovation.

The construction of the station is based on the experience gained from its precursors, Tiangong-1 and Tiangong-2. The first module, the Tianhe ("Harmony of the Heavens") core module, was launched on 29 April, 2021. This was followed by multiple crewed and uncrewed missions and the addition of two laboratory cabin modules. The first, Wentian ("Quest for the Heavens"), launched on 24 July, 2022; the second, Mengtian ("Dreaming of the Heavens"), launched on 31 October, 2022.
Mars Exploration:
Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and the second smallest planet in the Solar System after Mercury.
It is also known as Red Planet (due to presence of iron oxide on its surface).
It is a terrestrial planet with a thin atmosphere.
Its surface reminds the craters of Moon and volcanoes, valleys, deserts, and polar ice caps of the Earth.
Olympus Mons
is a very large shield volcano on the planet Mars. This volcano has a height of approximately 22 km as measured by the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter. It is about two and a half times of Mount Everest.
The largest canyon system situated on Mars is
Valles Marineris.
NASA launched Mariner 4 on 28 November, 1964; it flew by Mars on 14 July, 1965 and captured the first close-up images of a planet beyond Earth.
On 14 November, 1971 Mariner 9 entered the orbit around Mars and became the first space probe to orbit another planet.
After these mission several campaigns were conducted but twin rover
Spirit
and
Opportunity
and later rover
Curiosity
were highlighted, which were launched by NASA.
Perseverance
is the latest Mars rover of NASA.
Rover:
Rover means – wanderer/roamer.
In celestial reference, rover is such a vehicle, which is capable to rove on or move across the surface of a celestial body.
Rovers are created to land on any planet or celestial body to find out information and to take samples. They can collect dust, rocks and even take pictures.
They usually arrive at the planetary surface on a lander style spacecraft.
Spirit:
Spirit also known as MER-A (Mars Exploration Rover-A) or MER-2, is a robotic rover on Mars, active from 2004 to 2010.
It was one of two rovers of NASA's Mars Exploration Rover (MER) mission.
Opportunity:
It is also known as MER-B or MER-1 rover.
It is a robotic rover which was active on Mars from 2004 to June, 2018.
MER mission concluded when opportunity mission ended; announced in February, 2019.
Before it, under NASA'S Mars Pathfinder mission–
Sojourner
rover was arrived on Mars (in 1997) which was active only for three months.
Curiosity:
Curiosity is a car-sized rover designed to explore the Gale crater on Mars (as part of NASA's Mars Science Laboratory Mission) which was landed on Mars in August, 2012.
This rover is still (As of April, 2026) operational and exploring Mars.
Perseverance:
It is a car-sized Mars rover designed to explore the Jezero crater on Mars. It was launched on 30 July, 2020 and successfully landed on Mars on 18 February, 2021.
Following the rover's arrival, NASA named the landing site
Octavia E. Butler Landing
The rover Perseverance also carried the mini-helicopter '
Ingenuity

' to MARS, an experimental aircraft and technology showcase that made the first powered flight on another planet on 19 April, 2021. On 18 January, 2024, it made its 72nd and final flight at Mars, suffering damage on landing to its rotor blades, causing NASA to retire it.

The rover's goals include identifying ancient Martian environments capable of supporting life, seeking out evidence of former microbial life existing in those environments, collecting rock and soil samples, and testing oxygen production from the Martian atmosphere to prepare for future crewed missions.
Mangalyaan:
It was a mission of India.
The Mangalyaan was also called Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM).
It successfully got inserted into Mars orbit on 24 Sept., 2014.
It was launched on 5 November, 2013 by ISRO.

The objectives of this mission were primarily technological and include design, realisation and launch of a Mars Orbiter spacecraft capable of operating with sufficient autonomy during the journey phase; Mars orbit insertion / capture and in-orbit phase around Mars.
MOM carried five scientific payloads to study the Martian surface features, morphology, mineralogy and Martian atmosphere.
The Primary science objective of Methane Sensor for Mars (MSM) payload was to detect and measure methane concentration in Martian atmosphere (if it does exist) under clear sky conditions.
India made world record by successful installation of Mangalyaan as it is the first nation in the world to do so in its first attempt.
India became first Asian country by acquiring this achievement.
On 27 September, 2022, ISRO delibrated the spacecraft was non-recoverable, and had attained its end-of-life.
UAE's Mars Mission 'Hope':
UAE's Mars orbiter mission 'Hope' (Arabic: Misbar Al-Amal) was launched on 19 July, 2020 (UTC) from the Tanegashima Space Centre in Japan with a Japanese rocket.

The Hope orbiter went into orbit around Mars on 9 February, 2021 and UAE became the first Arab country and the fifth spacefaring entity (after the USA, the Soviet Union, Europe and India) to reach Mars and the second country to successfully enter Mars' orbit on its first try (after India).
Tianwen-1:

It is an interplanetary mission by the China National Space Administration (CNSA) to send a robotic spacecraft to Mars, consisting of: an orbiter, two deployable cameras, lander, remote camera, and the
Zhurong
rover.
The mission was launched on 23 July, 2020 and entered Martian orbit on 10 February, 2021.

On 14 May, 2021 (UTC), the lander/rover portion of the mission successfully touched down on Mars, making China the third nation (after the Soviet Union and the USA) to make a soft landing on and establish communication from the Martian surface.
On 22 May, 2021, the Zhurong rover drove onto the Martian surface and with the successful deployment of the rover, China became the second nation to accomplish this feat, after the USA.
In addition, China is the first nation to carry out an orbiting, landing and rovering mission on Mars successfully on its maiden attempt.
Tianwen-1 is also the second mission to capture audio recordings on the Martian surface, after USA's Perseverance rover.
The Zhurong rover lost contact in 2022 after failing to awake from a scheduled hibernation.
Artemis program:

The Artemis program is a Moon exploration program led by the United States' National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), aimed at returning humans to the Moon for the first time since Apollo 17 in 1972.
Under this program, the uncrewed Artemis I mission sent an Orion spacecraft to lunar orbit in 2022, while Artemis II sent four astronauts on a lunar flyby in 2026.
Artemis III, scheduled for 2027, is planned to test an HLS lunar lander in Earth orbit. The first lunar landing of the program is planned for the Artemis IV mission, targeted for 2028.
Afterward, NASA intends yearly lunar landings to develop a permanent base on the Moon, as a stepping stone to human missions to deeper space.
These missions seek to reestablish a human presence on the Moon and demonstrate technologies and business approaches needed for future scientific studies, including exploration of Mars.
Artemis I:
Artemis I
(November 16–December 11, 2022), formerly Exploration Mission-1 (EM-1), was an uncrewed Moon orbiting mission.
As the first major spaceflight of NASA's Artemis program, Artemis I marked the agency's return to lunar exploration after the conclusion of the Apollo program nearly five decades earlier.

It was the first integrated flight test of the Orion spacecraft and Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, and its main objective was to test the Orion spacecraft, especially its heat shield, in preparation for subsequent Artemis missions.
Artemis I mission (Orion CM-002 spacecraft) was launched from Launch Complex 39B at the Kennedy Space Center on 16 November, 2022.

After reaching Earth orbit, the upper stage carrying the Orion spacecraft separated and performed a trans-lunar injection before releasing Orion and deploying ten CubeSat satellites. Orion completed one flyby of the Moon on November 21, entered a distant retrograde orbit for six days, and completed a second flyby of the Moon on December 5.
The Orion spacecraft then returned and reentered the Earth's atmosphere with the protection of its heat shield, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean on 11 December, 2022.
Artemis II:
Artemis II

(April 1–11, 2026) was a crewed lunar flyby mission. It was the first crewed flight of the NASA-led Artemis program and the first crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in 1972. Artemis II was the second flight of the Space Launch System (SLS) and the first crewed flight of the Orion spacecraft, named Integrity by the crew.
The mission's primary goal was to validate the Orion spacecraft's systems, crew operations, and mission procedures ahead of sustained lunar exploration in future Artemis missions.
Artemis II mission (Orion CM-003 Integrity ESM-2 spacecraft) was launched from Launch Complex 39B at the Kennedy Space Center on 1 April, 2026.

Victor Glover (an African-American) became the first person of color, Christina Koch the first woman, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen the first non-U.S. citizen, and commander Reid Wiseman the oldest person to travel beyond low Earth orbit and around the Moon.
After launch, Artemis II gained widespread global attention for its achievements and inclusive crew, giving rise to the term Moon joy.

On flight day 6, Orion entered the Moon's sphere of influence, where lunar gravity became the dominant force shaping its trajectory. Orion flew around the Moon at a closest approach of about 4,067 miles (6,545 km) from the far-side lunar surface on April 6.
During their lunar flyby, the crew set the record for human distance from Earth, 252,756 miles (406,771 km), breaking Apollo 13's record of 248,655 miles (400,171 km).
During their flyby, the crew observed two unnamed craters which they proposed be named Integrity, after their spacecraft, and Carroll, after Wiseman's late wife, who died of cancer in 2020.

On flight day 10, Orion spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere and splashdown occurred on 11 April, 2026, UTC in the Pacific Ocean southwest of San Diego, California, where the U.S. Navy recovered the crew.
Artemis Accords:

The Artemis Accords is a series of non-binding bilateral arrangements between the United States government and other world governments that elaborates on the norms expected to be followed in outer space.

The accords are related to the Artemis program, an American-led effort to return humans to the Moon by 2028, with the ultimate goal of expanding space exploration to Mars and beyond. The program's stated long-term goal is to establish a permanent base on the Moon to facilitate human missions to Mars.

The Accords were signed on 13 October, 2020 by representatives of the national space agencies of eight countries: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States.

The Accords remain open for signature indefinitely, as NASA anticipates more nations joining. Additional signatories can choose to directly participate in Artemis program activities, or may agree simply to commit to the principles for responsible exploration of the Moon as set out in the Accords.

As of 26 January, 2026, sixty-one countries have signed the accords, including twenty-eight in Europe, fifteen in Asia (including India and Bangladesh), seven in South America, five in North America, four in Africa and two in Oceania.
International Lunar Research Station:
The International Lunar Research Station (ILRS) is a planned lunar base currently being led by Russian space agency Roscosmos and the China National Space Administration (CNSA).

The ILRS will serve as a comprehensive scientific experiment base built on the lunar surface or in lunar orbit that can carry out multi-disciplinary and multi-objective scientific research activities including exploration and utilization, lunar-based observation, basic scientific experiment and technical verification, and long-term autonomous operation.

On 9 March, 2021 China and Russia signed a Memorandum of Understanding between the Government of the People's Republic of China and the Government of the Russian Federation regarding cooperation for the construction of the International Lunar Research Station. Statements from Roscosmos and CNSA underline that the project will be open to all interested countries and international partners.

As of January, 2026, fourteen more countries have joined this initiative. These are: Venezuela, South Africa, Azerbaijan, Pakistan, Belarus, Bolivia, Djibouti, Ethiopia, Egypt, Thailand, Nicaragua, Serbia, Kazakhstan and Senegal.
Indian Lunar Exploration Missions:
I.
Chandrayaan-1

Chandrayaan-1, India's first mission to Moon, was launched successfully on 22 October, 2008 by PSLV-C11 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota. The mission included a lunar orbiter and the Moon Impact Probe (MIP).
The spacecraft was orbiting around the Moon at a height of 100 km from the lunar surface for chemical, mineralogical and photo-geologic mapping of the Moon.

After the successful completion of all the major mission objectives and more than 3400 orbits around the Moon, the mission was concluded when the communication with the spacecraft was lost on 29 August, 2009.
II. Chandrayaan-2
India's Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, GSLV MkIII (LVM3)-M1, successfully launched Chandrayaan-2 spacecraft on July 22, 2019 from Satish Dhawan Space Centre SHAR, Sriharikota.
Chandrayaan-2 mission comprised an Orbiter, Lander and Rover to explore the unexplored South Pole of the Moon. On August 20, 2019, Chandrayaan-2 was successfully inserted into lunar orbit.
While orbiting the Moon in a 100 km lunar polar orbit, on September 2, 2019,
Vikram
Lander (with
Pragyan
Rover) was separated from the Orbiter in preparation for landing. Vikram Lander descent was as planned and normal performance was observed upto an altitude of
2.1 km Subsequently communication from lander to the ground stations was lost on September 7, 2019.

The Vikram lander carrying the rover crash-landed and was destroyed upon impact with the Moon's surface. Pragyan, being onboard Vikram, was also destroyed. A successful soft landing would have made India the fourth country after the Soviet Union (USSR), United States and China to do so.

The Orbiter of this mission placed in its intended orbit around the Moon will enrich our understanding of the moon's evolution and mapping of the minerals and water molecules in Polar regions, using its eight state-of-the-art scientific instruments. The precise launch and mission management has ensured a long life of almost 7.5 years instead of the planned one year.
III. Chandrayaan-3
Chandrayaan-3 is a follow-on mission to Chandrayaan-2 to demonstrate end-to-end capability in safe landing and roving on the lunar surface.

The mission consists of a Vikram lunar lander and a Pragyan lunar rover similar to those launched aboard Chandrayaan-2 in 2019, as well as a propulsion module that carried the spacecraft from Earth orbit to lunar orbit.
It was launched by GSLV-MkIII (LVM3-M4) from SDSC, SHAR, Sriharikota on 14 July, 2023.

The spacecraft entered lunar orbit on 5 August, 2023 and became the first lander to touch down near the lunar south pole on 23 August, 2023, making India the fourth country to successfully land on the Moon.

IV. Chandrayaan-4 Mission
In September, 2024, the Union Cabinet chaired by the PM Narendra Modi has approved the Chandrayaan-4 mission.

Chandrayaan-4 mission, aims at developing and demonstrating key technologies required for returning to Earth after a successful lunar landing. This mission will also focus on collecting samples from the Moon and analyzing them on Earth.

Chandrayaan-4 is a critical step toward establishing India's capabilities for a human mission to the Moon, planned for 2040. The mission will showcase advanced technologies for docking, undocking, landing and returning safely to Earth, alongside lunar sample collection and analysis.

The successful soft landing of Chandrayaan-3 demonstrated vital technologies that only a few nations possess. Building on this, Chandrayaan-4 will focus on returning lunar samples safely to Earth, a critical capability in future manned missions.

The mission, managed by ISRO and expected to be completed within 36 months of approval, will have strong participation from industry and academia. All critical technologies will be developed indigenously, creating high employment potential and technological spin-offs for other sectors.

The total funding requirement is Rs. 2,104.06 crore, covering spacecraft development, two launch vehicle missions of LVM3, external deep space network support, and special tests for design validation.

ploration (LUPEX) Mission, a collaborative effort between India's Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and Japan's Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), is an innovative mission focused on investigating the Moon's south pole.
It is the fifth mission in the Chandrayaan series, focused on studying lunar volatiles (including water) near a Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) in the lunar south pole.
This mission represents a notable advancement in lunar research and has significant implications for future space endeavours, including the potential for a permanent human presence on the Moon.
Scheduled for launch in the late 2020s (2027-28), LUPEX will enhance our understanding of critical resources on the Moon's surface, particularly concentrating on water ice deposits.
In this partnership, JAXA is tasked with creating a sophisticated rover (Japan's Mitsubishi Heavy Industries

Furthermore, the mission will include instruments from NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA), allowing for a wide variety of scientific experiments and data collection.
The mission is planned to be launched by JAXA on the H3-24L launch vehicle.
The approval for the Chandrayaan-5 / LUPEX mission was received from Government of India on March 10, 2025, in the form of financial sanction.
Chandrayaan-5 / LUPEX mission will be one of the major short-term milestones in India’s lunar exploration odyssey, which envisions Indian Gaganyatris (astronauts) landing on the Moon by year 2040.
NISAR Satellite:

NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite is a joint Earth-observing mission between NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) with the goal to make global measurements of the causes and consequences of land surface changes using advanced radar imaging.
In 2014, NASA and ISRO signed a partnership to collaborate on and launch NISAR.
NISAR is the first satellite mission using two different radar frequencies (L-band and S-band) to measure changes in our planet's surface less than a centimeter across.
NASA provided the mission's L-band synthetic aperture radar, a high-rate communication subsystem for science data, GPS receivers, a solid-state recorder and payload data subsystem.
ISRO provided the spacecraft bus, the S-band radar, the launch vehicle and associated launch services.
NISAR was launched onboard GSLV-F16 launch vehicle on 30 July, 2025 from ISRO’s Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC), SHAR, Sriharikota.

NISAR is the first of its kind mission, jointly developed by ISRO and NASA. It is an Land S-band, global, microwave imaging mission, with capability to acquire fully polarimetric and interferometric data.

The unique dual-band Synthetic Aperture Radar of NISAR employs advanced, novel SweepSAR technique, which provides high resolution and large swath imagery. NISAR will image the global land and ice-covered surfaces, including islands, sea-ice and selected oceans every 12 days.
NISAR mission’s primary objectives are to study land & ice deformation, land ecosystems, and oceanic regions in areas of common interest to the US and Indian science communities.
NISAR mission will help to
 measure the woody biomass and its changes;
 track changes in the extent of active crops;
 understand the changes in wetlands’ extent;
 map Greenland’s & Antarctica’s ice sheets, dynamics of sea ice and mountain glaciers; and
 characterize land surface deformation related to seismicity, volcanism, landslides, and subsidence & uplift associated with changes in subsurface aquifers, hydrocarbon reservoirs, etc.
Aditya-L1 Mission:
On 2 September, 2023, the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV-C57) successfully launched the Aditya-L1 spacecraft, from the Second Launch Pad of Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC), Sriharikota.
Aditya-L1 is the first Indian space based observatory to study the Sun from a halo orbit around first Sun-Earth Lagrangian point (L1), which is located roughly 1.5 million km from Earth.

Aditya-L1 carries seven scientific payloads indigenously developed by ISRO and national research laboratories including Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru and Inter University Centre for Astronomy & Astrophysics (IUCAA), Pune.
On 6 January, 2024, Aditya-L1 was successfully injected on the Halo orbit of Lagrange point 1.

The instruments of Aditya-L1 are tuned to observe the solar atmosphere mainly the chromosphere and corona. In-situ instruments will observe the local environment at L1. There are total seven payloads on-board with four of them [Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT), Solar Low Energy X-ray Spectrometer (SoLEXS) and High Energy L1 Orbiting X-ray Spectrometer (HEL1OS)] carrying out remote sensing of the Sun and three of them [Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment (ASPEX), Plasma Analyser Package For Aditya (PAPA) and Advanced Tri-axial High Resolution Digital Magnetometers] carrying in-situ observation.
Aditya-L1 will provide a greater advantage of observing the solar activities and its effect on space weather in real time.

The suits of Aditya-L1 payloads are expected to provide most crucial informations to understand the problem of coronal heating, coronal mass ejection, pre-flare and flare activities and their characteristics, dynamics of space weather, propagation of particle and fields etc.

On 22 February, 2024, Aditya L1 captured the first-ever image of a X6.3-class solar flare 'kernel' occurring in the photosphere and the chromosphere. The image was taken by the SUIT instrument in the Near-Ultraviolet band (NUV), which operated alongside the SoLEXS and HEL1OS instruments to capture groundbreaking, detailed views of solar flares. On 16 July, 2024, the VELC instrument was used to measure a large Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) from the Sun. It also studied an accompanying solar flare and the motion of solar particles in the Sun's corona/outer atmosphere, tracking movement of solar material during the CME. Scientist from IIA reported on 20 April, 2025 observations of a flareless coronal mass ejection from reading taken by VELC in March, 2025.

Marking its first anniversary of injection into the halo orbit around L1, ISRO released the maiden set of the scientific data from the Aditya L1 to the global scientific community on 6 January, 2025 at the ISRO Headquarters in Bengaluru. ISRO presented the second set on 14 February, 2025.
Gaganyaan:

Gaganyaan project envisages demonstration of human spaceflight capability by launching crew of 3 members to an orbit of 400 km for a 3 days mission and bring them back safely to Earth, by landing in Indian sea waters.

The project is accomplished through an optimal strategy by considering inhouse expertise, experience of Indian industry, intellectual capabilities of Indian academia and research institutions along with cutting edge technologies available with international agencies.

The pre-requisites for Gaganyaan mission include development of many critical technologies including human rated launch vehicle for carrying crew safely to space, Life Support System to provide an Earth like environment to crew in space, crew emergency escape provision and evolving crew management aspects for training, recovery and rehabilitation of crew.

Various precursor missions are planned for demonstrating the Technology Preparedness Levels before carrying out the actual Human Space Flight mission. These demonstrator missions include Integrated Air Drop Test (IADT), Pad Abort Test (PAT) and Test Vehicle (TV) flights. Safety and reliability of all systems will be proven in unmanned missions preceding manned mission.

LVM3 rocket – The well proven and reliable heavy lift launcher of ISRO, is identified as the launch vehicle for Gaganyaan mission. It consists of solid stage, liquid stage and cryogenic stage. All systems in LVM3 launch vehicle are re-configured to meet human rating requirements and christened Human Rated LVM3. HLVM3 will be capable of launching the Orbital Module to an intended Low Earth Orbit (LEO) of 400 km.
Bharatiya Antariksh Station:
In September, 2024, the Union Cabinet chaired by the PM Narendra Modi has approved the building of first unit of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by extending the scope of Gaganyaan program.

The construction of the first module of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS-1) marks a significant expansion of the Gaganyaan program. This decision paves the way for missions aimedatdeveloping andvalidating the technologies required to build and operate the Indian space station. The revised scope of the Gaganyaan program will now include precursor missions for BAS, additional hardware requirements, and the inclusion of an additional uncrewed mission.

The Gaganyaan program, initially approved in December, 2018, was designed to launch human spaceflight missions to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and lay the groundwork for India's long-term ambitions in human space exploration.

The expanded vision of the Indian space program during Amrit Kaal includes establishing an operational Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035 and sending an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040. The program will involve eight missions, to be completed by 2028, including the launch of the first unit of BAS-1.

ISRO will lead the Gaganyaan program, working closely with industry, academia, and other national agencies. Four missions under the current Gaganyaan plan are expected by 2026, followed by four additional missions focused on demonstrating and validating technologies for the space station by December, 2028.
The revised Gaganyaan program now has a total funding allocation of Rs. 20,193 crore, with an additional Rs. 11,170 crore in newly approved funding.
SpaDeX Mission:

In a historic achievement, the Space Docking Experiment (SpaDeX) mission's docking operation was successfully completed on 16 January, 2025 marking India's entry into the elite group of nations capable of executing space docking operations.
With this success, India becomes the fourth country in the world to achieve this technological feat.

ISRO started the mission on 30 December, 2024, with the successful launch of the SpaDeX satellites (A&B; SDX 01 and SDX-02) using Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV)-C60, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota.

This groundbreaking mission aims to showcase India's technological prowess in spacecraft rendezvous, docking, and undocking – a critical capability for future advancements such as satellite servicing, space station operations, and interplanetary exploration.

On 16 January, 2025, the docking process was executed with exceptional precision. Post-docking, the integrated control of the two satellites as a single object has been successfully achieved, showcasing India's technological expertise.

As per PIB, India became the fourth country in the world to achieve this successful space docking after the USA, Russia, and China. However, Japan's ETS-VII (KIKU-7) also conducted rendezvous docking experiments earlier.

SpaDeX is a cost-effective technology demonstrator mission designed to showcase in-space docking using two small spacecrafts launched by 62nd PSLV flight. This mission is pivotal for India's future space ambitions, including lunar missions, sample returns, and the development of the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS). The main goals of the SpaDeX mission are:
w Develop and demonstrate technology for rendezvous and docking using two small spacecrafts.
w Showcase controllability in the docked condition. w Demonstrate the potential for extending the life of the target spacecraft.
w Test power transfer between docked spacecraft.

On 13 March, 2025, ISRO successfully undocked the SpaDeX satellites, a significant achievement demonstrating India's capabilities in rendezvous, docking and undocking operations in a circular orbit, paving the way for future missions like Chandrayaan-4 and a planned space station.

After successful undocking, the spacecraft separated and will be further used for application missions. During undocking, the spacecraft separated to begin individual payload operations. These payloads will provide high resolution images, natural resource monitoring, vegetation studies and on orbit radiation environment measurements which find numerous applications.

On 20 April, 2025, ISRO successfully demonstrated the docking of SDX-01 and SDX-02 spacecraft for the second time. On the next day, the electrical power transfer from SDX-02 and SDX-01 and vice versa was also completed successfully.

Space docking is a critical prerequisite for upcoming space missions, such as lunar exploration and the operation of space stations. By successfully executing this mission, ISRO is laying the foundation for autonomous docking – a vital capability for future missions like Chandrayaan-4. Additionally, the SpaDeX mission will play a key role in supporting India's ambitious space goals, such as the Gaganyaan mission, sending an Indian astronaut to the Moon and setting up the Bharatiya Antariksh Station.
LISA Project:
LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) is a formally adopted space mission to detect and accurately measure gravitational waves.
It is a space-based gravitational wave observatory building on the success of LISA Pathfinder and LIGO.
LISA is designed to detect milliHertz gravitational waves that cannot be observed by ground-based detectors.
The European Space Agency (ESA) is leading this mission with supports from NASA and an international consortium of scientists.

LISA is a spectacular plan of setting into space three spacecrafts, which will fly in a triangular formation, trailing the Earth in its orbit around the Sun at a distance of about 50 million km from Earth. Each arm of the imaginary equilateral triangle will measure around 2.5 million km.
The distance between the spacecrafts is precisely monitored by laser interferometers to detect a passing gravitational wave. This mission is slated to launch in 2035.
VERITAS and DAVINCI:

'VERITAS’ and 'DAVINCI' will be NASA's first missions to Venus since the 1990s. VERITAS is currently planned to launch no earlier than 2031 and will arrive at Venus after about six-month cruise, then enter polar orbit (DAVINCI has a tenative launch year of 2029/30). These missions are Part of NASA's Discovery Program.

The VERITAS (Venus Emissivity, Radio Science, InSAR, Topography, and Spectroscopy) mission will map the surface of the planet, study its geology, and hunt for volcanic activity. VERITAS – which means truth in Latin – will help scientists learn the facts about how Venus became a sulfurous inferno, while Earth evolved to become home to an abundance of life.

The DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging) will explore Venus using both gravity-assist flybys and a dedicated descent atmospheric probe. It will study the dense atmosphere of Venus to understand the trigger and evolution of the runaway greenhouse effect active on the planet.
Venus Orbiter Mission (VOM):
In September, 2024, the Union Cabinet chaired by the PM Narendra Modi has approved the development of Venus Orbiter Mission (VOM).

The ambitious Venus Orbiter Mission (VOM) marks a major step forward in India's planetary exploration efforts beyond the Moon and Mars. Venus, the closest planetary neighbor to Earth (at closest approach) and believed to have formed under conditions similar to our own, presents a unique opportunity to study how planetary environments can evolve in dramatically different ways. This mission aligns with the government's long-term vision of advancing space exploration capabilities.

The Venus Orbiter Mission, led by the Department of Space, will place a scientific spacecraft in orbit around Venus. The mission aims to improve our understanding of the planet's surface, subsurface, atmospheric processes, and the Sun's influence on its atmosphere. Investigating the causes behind Venus's transformation from a potentially habitable planet to its current state will provide crucial insights into the evolutionary paths of both Venus and Earth.

ISRO will oversee the development and launch of the spacecraft, following its well-established project management practices. The data collected from the mission will be shared with the scientific community, fostering further research.
The mission is expected for launch in March, 2028, offering significant scientific insights and various outcomes, particularly in answering unresolved questions about Venus.

The total approved budget for the Venus Orbiter Mission is Rs. 1,236 crore, with Rs. 824 crore allocated to spacecraft development. The cost includes development and realization of the spacecraft including its specific payloads and technology elements, global ground station support cost for navigation and network as well as the cost of launch vehicle.

Prithvi Missile:
Prithvi is a tactical surface to surface short-range ballistic missile developed by DRDO under the IGMDP. It is deployed by India’s Strategic Forces Command.
Its first test was conducted on 25 February, 1988 from (SHAR)- Sriharikota High Altitude Range.
Its variants are as follows –

RudraM-I:

The RudraM-I, previously referred as DRDO's anti radiation missile (ARM) or new generation anti-radiation missile (NGARM) is an air-to-surface anti-radiation missile developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).

It is primarily meant for suppression of enemy air defenses (SEAD), that can be launched from a range of altitudes with large standoffdistance for destroying enemy surveillance radars, tracking and communication systems.
It is the first indigenous anti-radiation missile developed by India.
It has a range of up to 200 km and it can be launched from altitudes of 500 m to 15 km. Its range varies based on launch conditions.

RudraM-II:

Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) successfully flight-tested the RudraM-II air-to surface missile from Su-30 MKI platform of the Indian Air Force (IAF) off the coast of Odisha on May 29, 2024.
The flight-test met trial objectives, validating the propulsion system and control and guidance algorithm.
RudraM-II is described as an indigenously-developed, solid-propelled, air-launched missle system meant for Air-to-Surface role to neutralise multiple types of enemy assets.
A number of state-of-the-art indigenous technologies developed by various DRDO laboratories have been incorporated in the missile system.
It has a range of 300 km and has an additional Imaging Infrared (IIR) seeker.
The missile can be launched from a variety of altitudes and has the capability to detect enemy radio frequencies and signals from radars at ranges exceeding 100 km.
It is equipped with Lock-On-Before/After-Launch systems, providing flexibility in targeting.
Additionally, the missile features an internal guidance system that enables it to autonomously navigate towards the target after launch.
Prahaar Missile:
Its weight is 1.28 Tonne with a length of 7.3 metre and diameter of 42 cm.

Amogha ATGM Missiles:
Amogha I
is a second generation, Anti-Tank, Guided Missile (ATGM) which has pinpoint accuracy for a range upto 2.8 km.
It has been designed and developed by Bharat Dynamics Ltd. (BDL) at Hyderabad.

The test firing was carried out on September 10, 2015 at Babina Army Range, Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh.

is an indigenous, third-generation, man portable ‘fire-and-forget’ Anti-Tank Guided Missile (ATGM) designed and developed by the in-house R&D Division of Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL).
On 7 February 2020, BDL unveiled Amogha-III ATGM at Defexpo 2020 in Lucknow.
It features a tandem warhead, dual-mode Imaging Infra Red (IIR) seeker, and a range of200 m to 2.5 km, capable of top and direct attack modes for destroying modern armored vehicles.
BDL successfully test-fired its Amogha-III ATGM on March 26, 2023. The test met all mission objectives, demonstrating fire-and-forget capability with a range of 200 m–2.5 km.

On 21 February, 2024, Indian Army's Battle Axe Division (12 Infantry Division, part of XII Corps) tested the 2.5 km range ATGM in Jaisalmer district. The missile was fired from man portable tripod. The missile uses a tandem high-explosive anti-tank (HEAT) warhead to neutralise vehicles with explosive reactive armour (ERA).
K- Missile Family:

The K-missile family named after Indian Scientist and former President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, is a series of submarine-launched ballistic missile developed by India to boost its second-strike capabilities and thus augments its nuclear deterrence.
First missile of this series is
Sagarika (K-15)
which has been tested successfully many times.

has been reported as a land-based version of Sagarika K-15 Missile.
